competitors.title: The 2026 Guide to Coding CLI Tools: 15 AI Agents Compared
key_points: 15 CLI coding tools compared across categories: Big-Lab Native (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI), Independent/Startup (Amp, Aider, Warp, Augment, Droid, Kiro), Open Source (OpenCode, Goose, Crush, Cline, Kilo)
Claude Code: highest autonomy, tied to Anthropic models, strong at complex refactors and multi-file changes
Codex CLI: lightweight, local-first, sandboxed execution, included with ChatGPT subscription
Gemini CLI: most generous free tier (60 req/min, 1000/day), 1M token context, Google Search grounding
Copilot CLI: native GitHub integration (issues, PRs, repos), multi-provider model support
Aider: 40K+ GitHub stars, 4.1M+ installs, supports virtually every LLM including local models via Ollama
OpenCode: 95K+ GitHub stars, 75+ LLM providers, privacy-first, multi-session support

competitors.title: Enterprise Controls for CLI Coding Agents: 2026 Field Guide
key_points: Multi-agent sprawl is default: enterprises with 500+ engineers have 3+ CLI agents in active use (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, Cline, Aider, Copilot)
Five control surfaces: Access control, Cost attribution, Audit logging, DLP on prompt egress, Model governance
Standardize the control plane, not the agent — let developers keep their chosen surface, make every agent answer to the same gateway hop
Virtual keys per developer (IdP broker) is standard pattern for access control; workload identity with short-lived tokens for regulated work
Session-level cost attribution identifies runaway sessions (e.g., one CI/CD agent retrying same 90K-token completion 6 times = 4% of spend)
Immutable trace store with policy-driven retention is the gold standard for audit logging
DLP needs tiered approach: pattern sync + async semantic for autocomplete, sync semantic for conversational agents
Model governance: allowlist with policy-driven routing and feedback-driven optimization produces 15-30% cost reductions

angles: Local vs remote: the fundamental architectural divide — local agents (Claude Code, Aider, Codex CLI) run on your machine with data privacy but limited compute; remote agents (Cursor Cloud Agents, Codex cloud) offer persistent execution and powerful infrastructure but raise data sovereignty concerns

Security and privacy tradeoffs: local agents keep code on-device (critical for regulated industries), remote agents process data in the cloud — the enterprise gateway pattern (FutureAGI, Portkey, LiteLLM) bridges this by routing all agents through a single control plane with DLP, audit logging, and access control

Cost comparison: local agents are pay-per-token (Claude Code ~$3/M input tokens) vs subscription models (Copilot CLI $10-19/month, Cursor $20/month) vs free tiers (Gemini CLI's retired free tier, OpenCode with local Ollama) — the right choice depends on usage volume and team size

The autonomy spectrum: from fully autonomous (Claude Code, Droid, Amp Deep mode) through balanced (Aider, Codex, Gemini CLI) to human-in-the-loop (Cline, Kiro spec-driven) — matching autonomy level to codebase sensitivity is the key decision

Enterprise multi-agent sprawl: most orgs have 3+ agents in active use — the winning strategy is standardizing the control plane (gateway), not the agent, with five control surfaces: access, cost, audit, DLP, and model governance

The convergence trend: MCP as universal tool protocol, permission tiering (read-only/ask/auto-approve), project instruction files (CLAUDE.md/GEMINI.md/AGENTS.md), and session persistence are becoming standard across all agents

Future outlook: cloud execution (Codex cloud, Cursor Cloud Agents) and agent-to-agent protocols (ACP, MCP server mode) point toward a future where the terminal is just the client for a distributed agent fleet
outline: Introduction: The CLI coding agent explosion of 2025-2026 — from autocomplete to autonomous agents
The Landscape: 15+ serious CLI coding agents across three categories (Big-Lab Native, Independent/Startup, Open Source)
Local vs Remote Architecture: What it means — local agents run on-device with privacy, remote agents execute in cloud with persistent infrastructure
Security and Privacy Tradeoffs: Data sovereignty, DLP on prompt egress, sandboxing approaches (OS-level vs worktree vs none), enterprise gateway patterns
Cost Analysis: Pay-per-token vs subscription vs free tiers — total cost of ownership for individuals, teams, and enterprises
The Autonomy Spectrum: From fully autonomous to human-in-the-loop — matching agent autonomy to codebase sensitivity and developer comfort
Enterprise Multi-Agent Sprawl: Why most orgs have 3+ agents and why standardizing the control plane beats standardizing the agent
The Five Control Surfaces: Access control, cost attribution, audit logging, DLP, and model governance — building a defensible multi-agent architecture
Convergent Patterns: MCP, permission tiering, project instruction files, session persistence — what every agent now does the same way
Divergent Bets: Sandboxing, hooks, skills portability, cloud execution, model portability — where agents disagree reveals what each vendor considers the hard problem
Decision Framework: How to choose based on model commitment, autonomy comfort, budget, and non-coding needs
Future Outlook: Cloud execution, agent-to-agent protocols (ACP, MCP server mode), and the terminal as client for a distributed agent fleet
Conclusion: The right agent depends on your threat model, budget, and workflow — but the architecture question matters more than the tool choice
